content: In countries with a high incidence of tuberculosis (TB), the quality of evidence for assessing the development of TB disease among household contacts of TB patients is limited due to the small number of studies available. Only data from studies conducted in high TB incidence settings with a follow-up period of 1–2 years were included in the analysis. One outlier study was excluded because of uncertainty regarding whether the cases included were co-prevalent or incident. Variability in TB incidence rates across studies likely reflects differences in background TB prevalence. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed consolidated guidelines on TB preventive treatment, which include evidence-to-decision tables. These guidelines emphasize the importance of excluding active TB before initiating preventive treatment, particularly in people living with HIV (PLHIV) who are on antiretroviral therapy (ART). Since 2011, WHO has recommended a four-symptom screening rule—current cough, weight loss, night sweats, and fever—to rule out active TB in PLHIV before starting TB preventive treatment (TPT). This approach has significantly expanded the use of preventive treatment globally, with nearly 1 million recipients in 2015. The addition of chest radiography (CXR) to the four-symptom screening rule has been shown to increase sensitivity (from 60% to 88% and 53% to 80%) but decrease specificity (from 55% to 26% and 55% to 37%). This means that while more cases of active TB are correctly identified, there is also an increase in false positives, leading to unnecessary investigations for individuals who do not have TB. The differences in sensitivity and specificity between screening methods were statistically significant. In high TB incidence settings, the use of symptom screening alone or in combination with CXR has been evaluated for its ability to exclude active TB before providing preventive treatment. For PLHIV on ART, the addition of CXR to symptom screening may reduce the number of false negatives (missed TB cases) but increases the number of false positives, requiring more individuals to undergo further investigations. This could place additional burdens on health systems and patients, particularly in resource-limited settings. The WHO guidelines recommend that CXR should not be a mandatory requirement for initiating TPT in PLHIV, as the marginal gain in negative predictive value does not justify the additional resource requirements. However, CXR may be offered to PLHIV on ART to enhance confidence in ruling out active TB, provided it does not create barriers to accessing preventive treatment. The guidelines also highlight the importance of good clinical practices to minimize risks, especially for vulnerable populations such as pregnant women and children. The systematic review conducted to assess the performance of the four-symptom screening rule and CXR in excluding active TB found moderate-quality evidence for true positives and high-quality evidence for true negatives. However, the overall certainty of the evidence was considered low due to imprecision and the small number of studies available. In summary, the WHO recommends the use of the four-symptom screening rule for all PLHIV at every health facility visit or contact with a health worker. CXR may be used selectively to rule out active TB before initiating TPT, but its routine use should be carefully considered based on local epidemiology, health infrastructure, and resource availability. Further research is needed to evaluate the performance and feasibility of these screening algorithms, particularly in children and pregnant women.
